All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

title: Necessary for What? Auditing Demographic Disclosure to LLM Synthetic Respondents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly answer surveys on behalf of real panelists, and each panelist's recorded demographic attributes (e.g., age, education, ethnicity) are often placed in the prompt on the premise that richer profiles make more faithful synthetic respondents. While data minimization limits personal data to what a purpose requires, a synthetic survey serves several purposes at once, from predicting individual answers to estimating how opinions are distributed and comparing groups. We ask which of these purposes require the respondent's record, and whether improved estimates support sound conclusions about groups. We vary whose profile a model receives, where it comes from, and how many fields it contains, in two U.S. surveys with eleven open-weight and three hosted models, and compare each model with a statistical model fit to the same information. We make four contributions. First, we show that the record adds little to individual predictions and that, for the open-weight models, most of its gain in population estimates remains when it is replaced by census data or a synthetic persona. Second, we find that group comparisons improve only with the respondent's own record, and that even then the models' group differences rest more on the demographic label in the prompt than on the individual respondent, which the usual check of reproducing known group differences does not reveal. Third, we find that the models make groups look more alike than they are, keeping differences in circumstances while flattening or reversing differences in attitudes, most sharply for religious affiliation and ethnic origin, both special categories of personal data. Fourth, we outline an audit that a survey organization can run on questions it has already fielded to decide which estimates may use the record.

title: BiGSyn: A Bi-Level Heterogeneous Graph Contrastive Learning Framework for Interpretable Drug Synergy Prediction
summary: Drug combination therapy has become a mainstream of modern medicine, with the potential to enhance efficacy, reduce toxicity, and overcome drug resistance. However, identifying synergistic drug combinations remains challenging, as it requires modeling complex interactions across multiple biological scales---from atom-level molecular structures to entity-level relations in biological networks. Existing approaches typically model these levels in isolation, overlooking complementary signals and long-range dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose BiGSyn, a Bi-level heterogeneous Graph contrastive learning framework for drug Synergy prediction. Specifically, BiGSyn leverages heterogeneous graph transformers to extract high-order dependencies from molecular graphs and biological networks, and introduces a bi-level contrastive learning objective to bridge the cross-level semantic gap. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that BiGSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, its attention mechanism highlights key molecular substructures and biological interactions driving synergy, providing interpretable insights.

title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures
summary: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one. We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

title: Scaling a Universal Graph Neural Network Force Field to Billions of Atoms on Desk-Side GPUs
summary: Machine-learning force fields are capable of simulating billions of atoms, but usually require high-performance supercomputing clusters. We show that a universal graph neural network force field, ALIGNN-FF, evaluates energies and forces of more than one billion atoms on desk-side computers such as the NVIDIA GB10, which has 128 GB of unified memory, by using a cube-and-halo decomposition. The halo contains every atom within the model's 20 Å receptive field, which makes the result exact. One GB10 holds 216,000 atoms with forces as a single graph. The cube-and-halo decomposition removes this limit, enabling an evaluation of 2 billion atoms on nine GB10s. We also demonstrate three case studies: a billion-atom polycrystal, a 102-million-atom microelectronic gate stack and a 1.07-million-atom satellite tobacco mosaic virus in water. This brings single-point evaluations at experimentally relevant sizes within reach of one research group. The code is available at: https://github.com/atomgptlab/scalingmat.

title: A Self-Evolving Agent Runs Like a Gas: Describing and Predicting Its Evolution with Fluid Dynamics
summary: A self-evolving LLM agent improves in service by rewriting its own plugin library under a validation gate. Agent engineering is converging on exactly such agents: single systems in continuous operation, carrying populations of runtime instances (plugins, skills, tools) past the point where anyone can read the library and still predict what the system will do. Yet the run itself, the aggregate motion of that population across hundreds of edit rounds, is unstudied: no theory says whether it relaxes, oscillates, or freezes. A recent kinetic theory supplies the missing level: under four architectural properties, the plugin instances of one agent behave as identical hard spheres whose density obeys a master equation, and the theory is candid that its gate injects and drains credit, momentum is not conserved, and waves are excluded by construction. We argue the boundary is architectural; keeping the four safety theorems, we stack conservation axioms on top. A closed-credit ledger makes credit a collision invariant and unlocks acoustic waves at a measurable, engineerable speed; a zero-sum projection gate conserves centroid momentum unconditionally, for any proposal stream. Both layers are proven and executed: the axis total is conserved to the digit over 66 interventions under a live gate, and the pre-registered decisive probe returns the theory's directional verdict: linear wavefronts where the ledger holds, dissipation where it does not, replicated across two population sizes. For agents that must never stop, the gas description is not a metaphor: it is the measurement interface through which their future becomes readable.

title: Relaxation Critical Dynamics of Strong-to-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking
summary: Strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB) is unique to mixed states: strong symmetry is broken while weak symmetry is preserved, requiring two order parameters. We study the critical relaxation of both order parameters in a monitored $\mathbb{Z}_2$ circuit, which maps exactly onto two nested bond-percolation problems. The initial state acts as a temporal boundary condition for each problem, wired if the state is ordered in the corresponding order parameter and free otherwise. An SW-SSB initial state wires only the strong-symmetry order parameter, a configuration that no pure state realizes. Each autocorrelation exponent is the sum of an initial scaling dimension, set by the initial state, and an observation dimension, set by the observation time, whereas the equal-time correlator gives only the observation dimension. For the SW-SSB state, the initial dimension is $1/3$ for the weak-symmetry order parameter and $0$ for the strong-symmetry one, each at its own critical point. These initial dimensions also set how fast a stored bit is lost. The probability of decoding the initial value of a single qubit from the system alone decays as a power law, whereas system and environment together retain it. Stabilizer simulations confirm the theoretical prediction, and we propose an experimental protocol that measures these exponents without postselection. Our results reveal a form of boundary criticality inaccessible to pure states.

title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

title: Dynamic Shaping: Acquiring Interfaces and Constructing Execution over Frozen Pretrained Components
summary: We introduce Dynamic Shaping, a method for constructing executable neural arrangements through acquired response and partial-derivative interfaces over frozen pretrained components. The method learns local descriptions of available computation, ranks component rebindings using task-gradient alignment, transports the current interface across a rebinding, and retains changes through behavioral feedback. Continuous interface acquisition uses proximal policy optimization; the source coefficients remain fixed. We derive an exact identity relating transport error in component responses and partials to changes in action logits and their sensitivities. A pixels-only ViZDoom Basic study evaluates first task acquisition without a competent reference controller, demonstrations or intact response targets. Across three initializations and 100 shared held-out game seeds, initial arrangements succeed on 86/300 controller/episode pairs; joint interface-and-binding construction succeeds on 295/300. Fixed-binding interface acquisition also reaches 295/300. Each policy executes four source fragments, with 110 acquired interface values and fixed random visual and action projections. The artifact includes all candidate trials, interventions and costs; all 1,200 recorded initial/retained outcomes replay exactly. The contribution is an explicit profile, rebind, transport and retain procedure and a reproducible reference-free acquisition case over frozen pretrained computation.

title: Nonsense rank correlations between independent random walks
summary: Yule's nonsense correlation persists for Spearman's rho and Kendall's tau between independent random walks. Neither coefficient concentrates at zero as the sample size grows. For centred random walks with finite increment variances, we derive a universal joint limit expressed through Brownian occupation functionals. Integral formulas give limiting variances of approximately 0.222 and 0.108, respectively, below the Pearson value of 0.241. Rank correlations thus reduce the limiting dispersion on their respective coefficient scales. We prove that both marginal limits have symmetric densities and represent them exactly as limits of polynomial densities determined by Gaussian moment integrals. Spearman's conventional t test and Kendall's normal approximation are asymptotically invalid, with rejection probabilities tending to one under process independence.

title: Stability threshold of Couette flow for two-dimensional MHD equations on the infinite channel
summary: In this paper, we study the stability threshold of the two-dimensional incompressible MHD equations near Couette flow and a constant horizontal magnetic field \((β,0)\) on \(\mathbb T\times\mathbb R\). For \(N>10\), \(0<ν,μ\le1\) and \(|β|\ge(ν+μ)/(3\sqrt{νμ})\), we prove global stability for initial perturbations of size \(δ_N\min\{ν,μ\}^{1/3}\) in \(H^N\), where \(δ_N>0\) is independent of \(ν,μ,β\). We also obtain enhanced dissipation of the nonzero horizontal modes on the time scale \(\min\{ν,μ\}^{-1/3}\), together with inviscid damping of the vertical components. The proof combines time-dependent Fourier multipliers with an energy correction constructed using the Alfvén oscillations. By combining the nonlinear terms arising from this correction, we obtain the cancellation needed to close the energy estimates at the $1/3$ scale.

title: ToolGraph as a Q-Function for Test-Time Scaling of Tool-Use Agents
summary: Tool-use agents must chain interdependent calls, yet which outputs satisfy which later inputs in a deployed catalog is not something a general-purpose language model reliably infers from tool descriptions alone. We compile that structure once into a reusable external representation. ToolGraph is a directed, weighted dependency graph over a tool catalog: parameter matching and interventional probes, which execute a candidate chain with and without its proposed predecessor, propose edges whose evidence is combined into an edge confidence. Prior work uses such graphs to retrieve tools, search for tool paths, or score the next call. We ask instead whether the same structure can supply a \emph{multi-step} value by composing graph paths into a goal-conditioned action value \(Q(s,a,g)\). We study three estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, a GraphSAGE estimator distilled from it, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) plus a verbalizer that returns action--goal feedback to the agent, which keeps final action selection. Across two tool-use benchmarks and three backbones, we compare value ranking against personalized-PageRank retrieval over the identical graph, and against direct and reflective agents. Composition pays off only when the estimator also reads the concrete state: the LLM estimator improves on PageRank in every benchmark--backbone setting, by \(8.3\) points on average, while the two purely structural estimators fall below it, because a value defined over tool types cannot separate a correct tool called with a wrong argument. Graph construction is a one-time cost; we report it separately rather than assume it amortized away (at our scale it is comparable to request-time cost) and sweep four knobs controlling how much graph evidence to expose against success and tokens.

title: sqrtVINS-Based 360 Visual-Inertial SLAM Systems: Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge 2026 Entry
summary: This report describes our submission to the 2026 Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge. The system is a 360-camera visual-inertial pipeline that uses only the provided dual-fisheye image streams and IMU measurements. First, raw images are preprocessed with low-light enhancement and static/dynamic masking, and then fed into a $\sqrt{\text{VINS}}$ frontend as the local odometry, with deep learning-based SuperPoint features, ELSED line segments, and LightGlue matching. The resulting trajectory is refined using a GTSAM-based backend that performs tightly-coupled factor graph optimization with SALAD global descriptor and visual bundle adjustment (BA). The backend performs local-to-global structureless BA, tightly regularized intrinsic and extrinsic refinement, and global scale adjustment supported by the known inter-camera baseline and cross-view constraints. The design targets long indoor sequences with dark regions, repetitive corridors, dynamic objects, and limited geometric parallax, while keeping the pipeline reproducible in the provided ROS2 workspace. Fig. 1 demonstrates that our proposed method aligns well with the floorplan across several indoor sequences.

title: Calibrated Functional Prediction from Overlapping Nonlinear Observations
summary: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for overlapping tasks, repeated row identities, and cross-row dependence. Shared-state residual samples extend this kernel through a positive-semidefinite feature representation. Positive matrix integration and sample-value enclosures connect the original inputs to the actual saved hybrid prediction. A sorted calibration-role perturbation bound then certifies its complete finite-pool pinball risk. Independent complete-loss selection chooses the ridge, score scale, and residual weight, while task-rank calibration supplies an upper endpoint. Evaluation uses twenty new reference contexts per dataset at two task sizes, giving 400 conditions across ten benchmark populations. The mean dataset complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 to the retrospective minimum over 174 public configurations. The last ratio has a paired reference-bootstrap interval of [0.9898,0.9927]. On 40 profiles at coefficient tolerance $10^{-7}$, Gamma quadrature has a geometric mean cold-time ratio of .0646 to strengthened Arb/Petras integration.

title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
summary: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.

title: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing
summary: Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models by replacing model generations with user-provided responses. Existing editors assume a single target answer for each edit. However, many real tasks inherently entail uncertainty, resulting in multiple plausible answers with varying likelihoods in user feedback. Such feedback forms a target distribution to not only correct but also calibrate model generations. We therefore propose SoftEdit, the first model editor to leverage uncertainty in user responses and perform one-shot calibration during editing. To generalize calibration to unseen samples, SoftEdit uses co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts, balancing the new distributional generality-locality tradeoff. Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, ultimately showing that uncertainty in user responses enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer corrections.

title: Bending Rigidity of Smectic Filaments
summary: Many biological and engineered filaments exhibit internal structure or fluidity that alters their elastic behavior. We study the elasticity of microscale filamentous smectic condensates, grown during liquid-liquid crystal phase separation. We use a Fourier analysis of their thermal bend fluctuations to measure their persistence length, which follows a non-classic linear scaling with their cross-sectional area, in contrast to the classic quadratic scaling for elastic filaments. We rationalize this scaling using the Helfrich energy to compute the free energy of bending a filament with internal smectic fluid ordering. Our analysis then provides a direct method to measure the bend modulus K, which quantifies the rigidity of smectic layers; providing the first method to directly measure K for dispersed smectic phases. We quantify the softening of filaments in the presence of shorter alkyl-tail mesogen dopants, decreasing K by up to ~35%. Out results suggest how nanoscale smectic organization and molecular composition determine filament-scale elasticity, informing the control of filament mechanics and self-assembly in biomimetic and engineered materials.

title: Learning a Task-Adaptive Low-Dimensional Semantic Space for Improved Visual Classification
summary: Semantic visual classification commonly aligns visual embeddings with semantic spaces induced by pretrained text encoders. However, such spaces are typically high-dimensional, weakly aligned with visual feature geometry, and insufficiently discriminative for downstream classification tasks. We propose TaSS, a framework for learning a task-adaptive low-dimensional semantic space that preserves semantic structure while explicitly optimizing class separability. TaSS is constructed through a parameterized geometry transformation of pretrained text embeddings that enlarges inter-class margins via distance reshaping and improves intra-class compactness through prototype-preserving semantic constraints. The resulting semantic space maintains meaningful semantic relationships while producing a discriminative geometry tailored for classification. Frozen visual encoder features are subsequently aligned to TaSS using a lightweight MLP, enabling improved discriminative learning without fine-tuning pretrained backbones. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that TaSS preserves semantic consistency while enforcing enhanced inter-class separation and controlled intra-class variance. Extensive experiments on skeleton-based human action recognition, video classification, and image classification benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing semantic alignment approaches, with gains exceeding 3 percentage points on average and up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.

title: GranularGPT: Natural-Language-Driven End-to-End Discrete Element Method Simulations
summary: Discrete element method (DEM) simulations are widely used to investigate granular and particulate systems, but their application often requires specialized expertise in particle physics, numerical modelling, and simulation post-processing. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to simplify these workflows by enabling users to interact with simulation tools through natural language. This study offers GranularGPT, an LLM-assisted agentic framework for end-to-end DEM simulation workflows, from natural-language problem descriptions to simulation execution and automated post-processing. The framework enables users to generate DEM simulation cases, execute and monitor simulations, and automatically extract and report physical and process-level metrics. Evaluation across 60 normal-condition cases covering 12 DEM scenarios and parameter variations achieve a simulation success rate of 91.7%. In the error-handling evaluation, all 10 repairable errors are detected and 9 are successfully resolved, while all 5 non-repairable cases are correctly identified and reported. The framework automatically extracts a range of DEM-relevant metrics, including particle size distributions, packing and density measures, velocity profiles, discharge rates, mixing indices, contact force characteristics, and thermal quantities. GranularGPT provides a foundation for improving the accessibility and efficiency of DEM simulation workflows while reducing the specialized expertise required for their operation.

title: RoShift: Lazy Shift and Weight-aware Rotation for Activation Sparsity in LLM Inference
summary: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at https://github.com/hulahula3247/RoShift

title: A Gaussian Primitive Data Management Framework for Efficient 3DGS Trajectory Rendering
summary: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.

title: Hyperspectral imaging from diffractograms
summary: We consider an optical system with a periodic point spread function, such as a camera with a periodic diffractive filter array placed near the sensor. Such systems produce a monochrome image that we call ``diffractogram'', and that multiplexes the spatial and spectral information about the scene. We present a method to efficiently invert this forward model and recover the hyperspectral scene. The inverse problem is formulated as a large scale $\ell_1$-penalized least squares problem that is solved iteratively with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). A Krylov subspace solver, such as LSQR, may require tens to hundreds of iterations to approximatively solve the augmented least-squares problem required in each ADMM iteration. Here we present an exact direct solver for the augmented least-squares problems that exploits the periodicity of the point spread function. Each direct solve costs roughly as much as three LSQR iterations, eliminating inner iterations entirely. We validate the method on both synthetic and experimental datasets.

title: PeV Gamma-Ray Emitters: Observations and Implications
summary: The origin of Galactic cosmic rays (CRs) around and beyond the knee remains an open problem. Gamma rays extending to the PeV range provide direct evidence for extreme particle acceleration. LHAASO has greatly expanded the observational sample of such sources. In this review, we use the term "PeV gamma-ray emitter" for a source whose measured spectrum extends to, or approaches, 1 PeV, rather than restricting it to sources detected above 1 PeV at more than $5σ$. We review LHAASO observations of six PeV gamma-ray emitters (i.e., the Crab Nebula, the Aquila Booster, the Cygnus Bubble, Cygnus X-3, V4641 Sgr, and GRS 1915+105) together with relevant multiwavelength observations and on-going theoretical studies. Together, these sources show that PeV particle acceleration can occur in different environments and on spatial scales ranging from compact pulsar-wind nebulae and binary-scale jets to large-scale jet--environment interaction regions and extended star-forming complexes. Their spectra, morphologies, variability, magnetic fields, and surrounding gas provide important constraints on particle acceleration and transport mechanisms. We also discuss the implications of these observations for the origin of Galactic PeV CRs and future observational prospects for clarifying this problem.

title: Scale-aware composite forcing enhances forward energy transfer in lattice Boltzmann simulations of forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence
summary: In forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence (FHIT), conventional large-scale forcing sustains statistical stationarity but offers limited control over energy at intermediate scales. We propose a scale-aware composite forcing strategy for the lattice Boltzmann method, combining large-scale random forcing with feedback aligned with an intermediate-scale velocity field extracted by composite filtering. The magnitude of the cross-power spectrum between feedback and filtered velocity is concentrated in the target band, with a time-averaged fraction of 72.26%-74.56%. Feedback increases energy in both target and high-wavenumber bands, with larger relative gains at high wavenumbers. At feedback strengths $α$ = 1%, 3%, 5%, and 7%, the target-band energy fraction increases by 6.29%, 11.65%, 18.99%, and 19.89% relative to the baseline. The mean forward nonlinear energy flux across K = 12 rises to 1.18, 1.54, 2.32, and 3.06 times its baseline value, with larger relative increases than across K = 4. As $α$ increases from 0% to 7%, the mean Taylor-microscale Reynolds number rises from 73.94 to 97.86 and enstrophy increases by 181.98%, while longitudinal velocity-gradient skewness shifts toward zero and standardized velocity and normalized Q'-R' distributions largely retain their shapes. Mean $k_{\max}η$ values of 1.01 and 0.90 at 5% and 7% feedback indicate an approaching resolution limit and a risk of under-resolution, respectively. At approximately matched dissipation rates, 5% feedback gives a target-band energy fraction of 32.36%, versus 27.55% under enhanced large-scale forcing, and a post-transient forward flux across K = 12 generally 2.17-2.39 times larger. The strategy thus enables targeted control of energy distribution and nonlinear transfer, with feedback strength constrained by small-scale resolution.

title: Effective and Efficient Rumor Assertion Over Large-Scale Social Networks (Technical Report)
summary: Nowadays, social networks, like Facebook, X, Reddit, YouTube, and so on, have become essential online platforms for users to connect with friends daily, post/share news, and express their opinions/comments. Meanwhile, however, the rapid and widespread dissemination of rumors and misinformation across social networks has become a serious concern. Such misleading information can distort public opinion and potentially cause significant social and economic consequences in real-world scenarios, including product promotion, elections and voting, and even cyberbullying. Therefore, accurately and efficiently verifying whether news spread on social networks is rumor or truth has become an increasingly important yet challenging problem. While previous works usually identified rumors by their contents, in this paper, we propose a novel \textit{user behavior model} to capture the users' judgment/discriminative abilities, which is learned via our well-designed evidence-aware probability reconstructor. We develop a general framework for tackling \textit{rumor assertion over large-scale social networks} (RA-SN), which can efficiently and effectively determine whether a given news item is a rumor with high confidence, based on users' behaviors, in a scalable manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed RA-SN approach on both real-world and synthetic graphs.

title: RemeshingAgent: An Iterative Agent for Repair-Based Decimation of Generated Building Meshes
summary: Aggressively simplifying a generated high-poly building mesh to 0.5-1% of its faces confronts a hard limit. The surface looks complete, yet the mesh is topologically shattered: 10^3-10^4 connected components and non-manifold thin walls. Below a certain budget, every practical decimator "melts": it deletes parts, welds thin walls, or breaks the error tolerance. We attribute this to instance-specific pathology: which components are significant and where the cliff sits vary from mesh to mesh, so no single fixed algorithm suffices, and decimation becomes an iterative loop of cleaning, simplifying, and verifying. We present RemeshingAgent, an agent that turns this loop into a validated process. The melting follows from a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms: below the component floor, no output satisfies the repair contract, and cleaning first is the theory-mandated response. At a 0.5% budget the agent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, and on the 24 training buildings a nine-participant single-workstation blind study prefers our outputs 168:48 (p = 0.0195, subject-level sign test). The trained skill deploys as retrieval replay: 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU, with no LLM calls.

title: ReconPotBench: Evaluating LLM Honeypots in Multi-Round Linux Reconnaissance
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to build interactive honeypots, yet existing evaluations mainly assess isolated command outputs and cannot determine whether a system remains believable when later commands depend on earlier results. We present ReconPotBench, a multi-round benchmark for Linux reconnaissance honeypots. It contains 1{,}032 three-round reconnaissance interactions across eight reconnaissance categories, with reference outputs collected from a real Linux environment. Under a unified testing protocol, we compare Cowrie, open-source LLMs, and closed-source LLMs along three dimensions: round-level authenticity, cross-round contextual consistency, and hacker-oriented reconnaissance value. Results show that multi-round evaluation exposes failures hidden by single-round testing, as authenticity declines with interaction depth and both open-source and closed-source LLMs struggle to maintain coherent state across rounds. LLM-based honeypots nevertheless outperform Cowrie in authenticity and reconnaissance value, while Cowrie remains more consistent because of its rigid templated behavior. Category-level analysis further shows that tasks requiring systems to preserve network relationships across rounds are harder than tasks centered on explicit entities such as ports. ReconPotBench enables reproducible evaluation of LLM honeypots across authenticity, entity consistency, and hacker-perspective utility in dependent multi-round interactions. The dataset is available at: https://github.com/qianli-wang/ReconPotBench

title: GaugeRoPE: RoPE-Compatible Executable Latent Attention
summary: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.

title: What the Averages Hide: Monocular Metric Depth Models Still Fail in Everyday Scenes, Mostly on Scale
summary: Zero-shot monocular metric depth models are evaluated by averaging metric and scale-aligned scores across datasets. Averages cannot show how many images still have severely wrong metric depth, whether depth is under- or overestimated, or whether different models fail on the same images. We propose an evaluation built on per-image results: the failure rate (metric $δ_1$ < 0.5); scale-aligned metrics for structure, and the bias, dispersion and absolute error of the alignment scale for scale; and a cross-model comparison that separates shared from model-specific failures. We apply it to 11 recent architectures with and without ground-truth intrinsics (18 model evaluations) on the 7 everyday-scene benchmarks (4,406 images) used by MoGe-2. Metric depth estimation is not solved in everyday scenes, and the remaining difficulty is mainly scale: the best of the 18 evaluations still has a failure rate of 7.7% (datasets weighted equally); pooled over all failures, 78.8% have intact structure, and after scale correction 98.3% no longer fail. Images failed by at least 6 architectures make up 7.3% of the data, concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; even when selected only by architectures of other families, they hold 34% to 40% of the error of the top 6 models, against 14% to 18% for as many random images from the same datasets. Adding objects reduces the scale error of most models; ground-truth intrinsics and, in most families, larger models reduce the failures but do not remove them. We recommend reporting failure rates, structure and scale separately, and results stratified by how many models fail. We will release the code, the per-image results with shared-failure labels, and two diagnostic sets built from TUM RGB-D.

title: Beyond the Patch: Reconstructing an Incomplete-Fix Patch Bypass in LLM Agent Frameworks with Control-Gated, Benign Probes
summary:
Replaying a vulnerability's original proof-of-concept after patching tests whether its reported trigger remains reproducible, but does not establish that the underlying security invariant holds on other code paths. We present a benign, control-gated reconstruction method and a pilot study across four LLM agent frameworks and four invariant classes. For PraisonAI, we compare original-trigger replay (B0) with a distinct sibling-path probe (M). We also perform five before/after reconstructions across Langroid, Agno, and CrewAI.
  Each run reports VIOLATION, NO_VIOLATION_OBSERVED, or INCONCLUSIVE, gated by a positive authorized control. Probes use inert markers or builtins-reachability checks. At PraisonAI 4.6.31, the original tool-loading trigger is blocked while the tool_override path still violates the invariant. This reproduces the publicly documented CVE-2026-44334 bypass of CVE-2026-40287; neither tested path shows a violation at 4.6.32. For CrewAI, we observe a violation in tested release 1.11.0 and confinement in 1.11.1, without claiming the earliest fixed release. Fourteen harness-validation scenarios produced their expected verdicts.
  Only one same-version B0-versus-M divergence is demonstrated. The PraisonAI probes invoke loader functions directly and establish boundary behavior under the supplied setup, not a full end-to-end exploit. A non-violation verdict applies only to the tested probe, version, and configuration and is not a proof of safety. This pilot reconstructs a known incomplete fix; it neither introduces a new testing technique nor estimates vulnerability prevalence.

title: Optimizing Query Decomposition for Reliable Validation
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have made querying databases more accessible, but cannot guarantee that the SQL they generate is correct. Without a trusted reference query, a validator (human or LLM) must decide whether a generated query answers the intended question. Enterprise questions often require queries with multiple joins, nested subqueries, and multi-level aggregation, and validating such a query in one judgment is error-prone. Decomposition simplifies this task by rewriting a query into smaller queries (blocks) that recompose to the original, each checked against its own sub-question.
  Decompositions differ, however: smaller blocks make each judgment easier but require more judgments, and the best balance depends on the validator's ability. We formulate validation-aware query decomposition as an optimization problem. Just as a query optimizer chooses among equivalent plans by estimated cost, we choose among decompositions by how reliably a given validator is expected to check them. We model how task difficulty and validator ability jointly affect reliability and define an objective that balances reliability against the number of judgments. Over a space of decompositions derived from logical-plan rewrites, our search finds an optimal one. We implement it in DecoVal, a pipeline that presents each block with its sub-question and input interface, combines local verdicts into a query-level decision, and localizes errors to blocks.
  A user study shows that decomposition helps human validators catch and locate errors: with DecoVal, participants caught 91% of the errors, up from 36% without decomposition, and located the error in nearly every rejection. Experiments on BEAVER and Spider 2.0 with LLM validators show that DecoVal also raises error-detection recall over whole-query validation while keeping precision high, and that the best granularity depends on the validator.

title: Quantum Sensing of Defects
summary: Metrology of defects (or impurities) is a major challenge in quantum sensing, with implications for material science, nano-scale metrology, and the development of high-precision quantum devices. In this work, we employ single and multi excitation sensors for the metrology of defects, with the system Hamiltonian encoding the structure of the sensor and the defect treated as a perturbation potential. We evaluate the quantum Fisher information of the ground state of the system to quantify the metrological performance of the sensors in locating a defect and in estimating its coupling strength. In doing so, we identify two distinct sensing regimes, determined by the ratio between the defect screening parameter and the inter-sensor site spacing, and establish the scaling behavior for the resulting estimation precision. Furthermore, we analyze the joint estimation of defect position and strength as well as the performance of two-excitation sensors, demonstrating how the number of excitations and their interactions influence sensitivity. Our results provide tools for optimizing defect detection with quantum sensors, with potential applications in solid-state quantum technologies.

title: VoxSAOR: Semantic-Aware Occupancy Robustification via Aleatoric Uncertainty Modeling
summary: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction provides a dense semantic representation of scenes for autonomous driving and embodied perception, yet remains vulnerable to occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection errors that induce spatially varying reliability in voxel features. Existing methods typically map voxel representations to semantic predictions without explicitly modeling such observation-induced feature variations. To address this limitation, we propose VoxSAOR, a semantic-aware occupancy robustification framework that models aleatoric uncertainty through feature-space proxies. It first quantifies Local Semantic Consistency (LSC) to derive a voxel-wise structural stability prior and uses cross-view semantic consensus to filter unreliable semantic correspondences. Within each semantic category, spatially matched stable and ambiguous voxels form stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions, which are modeled by a class-conditional diagonal Gaussian distribution, capturing both feature displacement and dispersion. Guided by these proxy distributions, Aleatoric Regime Ensemble Learning (AREL) trains independently parameterized prediction heads using feature perturbations at progressively increasing scales, with perturbation strength modulated by structural reliability. At inference, proxy modeling and sampling are disabled, and all heads process the same observed features; their output probabilities are then averaged to produce a deterministic consensus prediction without requiring sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and occupancy backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of VoxSAOR in improving semantic occupancy prediction, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/MengfeiD/VoxSAOR.

title: How Reliable Is Visual Token Selection? Rethinking Pruning in Multimodal LLMs
summary: Visual token pruning improves the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by removing redundant visual tokens, yet the reliability of existing selection signals has not been systematically examined. We analyze token selection under semantics-preserving perturbations and across representative pruning criteria, revealing two limitations. First, attention-based importance shifts non-uniformly under perturbations, so magnitude alone cannot distinguish stable evidence from unstable saliency (local instability). Second, attention- and diversity-based methods select substantially different subsets despite comparable performance, showing that useful evidence is not confined to a unique subset (global inconsistency). These findings motivate reliable token-set construction. We instantiate this perspective in CoRePruner, a training-free framework combining instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention. Across image benchmarks, multiple MLLM architectures, and token budgets, CoRePruner improves performance, especially under aggressive pruning, and remains competitive on video benchmarks. Our results establish reliability as a central consideration in visual token selection.

title: Scale profile, nesting, and the $A_2$ growth of dyadic paraproducts
summary: For the dyadic paraproduct $π_b$ and $Q\ge1$, let $Φ_b(Q)$ be the supremum of $\|π_b\|_{L^2(w)}$ over dyadic weights with $[w]_{A_2^d}\le Q$. Beznosova's linear bound $Φ_b(Q)\lesssim Q\,\|b\|_{\mathrm{BMO}_d}$ is sharp over $\mathrm{BMO}_d$, while every nonzero symbol safisfies $Φ_b(Q)\gtrsim Q^{1/2}$. We ask which properties of a fixed symbol place its growth between these extremes, and identify two: the distribution of the Haar coefficients of $b$ over scales and the nesting of their supports. Symbols supported on $L$ consecutive scales obey a two-weight bound of order $\sqrt L$; as a consequence, polynomial decay of the scale tails determines the sharp trowth exponent, except at a critical rate where the growth is determined up to a factor $(\log Q)^{1/2}$. For symbols supported on a chain, $\sup_Q Q^{-1/2}Φ_b(Q)$ is comarable to $\|S_d b\|_{\infty}$, and for every symbol the boundedness of the dyadic square function $S_d b$ is necessary for minimal growth $Q^{1/2}$. Conversely, $Φ_b(Q)\lesssim Q^{3/4}\|S_d b\|_{\infty}$ for every symbol, and the bound $\|π_b\|_{L^2(w)}\lesssim [w]_{A_2^d}^{1/2}\|S_d b\|_{i\infty}$ holds for every symbol at weights whose local $A_2$ imbalance has bounded evergy off a family of dyadic chains with disjoint tops; this class contains all weights used in our lower bounds.

title: PromptPoseFX: Authoring Pose-Driven Visual Effects through Augmented Prompting and Interactive Refinement
summary: Human pose-driven visual effects offer a compelling way for enhancing video expressiveness and storytelling. Authoring such effects with traditional video editing tools is a complex and time-consuming task that requires considerable technical expertise and manual effort. While generative AI models can simplify the workflow by reducing manual scripting through language-driven generation, existing approaches suffer from imprecise alignment between visual effects and pose data, failure to preserve original video content, and limited support for fine-grained, iterative refinement. To address these challenges, we present PromptPoseFX, an interactive system that allows creators to author pose-driven visual effects through augmented language prompts and interactive refinement. Our system leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate high-level user intent into parameterized procedural graphics scripts, automatically mapping pose-tracking data to specific effect parameters, allowing precise alignment with human motion. This script-based approach manages effects as independent layers, thereby preserving the original content of the underlying video. To reduce language ambiguity, our interface offers controls across spatial, temporal, and parameter domains, enabling the precise, intuitive, and iterative authoring of pose-driven visual effects. We evaluated PromptPoseFX through a comparative study against a text-only LLM interface, followed by an exploratory study. In the comparative study, participants rated PromptPoseFX significantly higher than the text-only baseline on measures of perceived control and precision. The exploratory study examined usability and creativity support in open-ended authoring tasks.

title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
summary:
SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics.
  We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.

title: Parallelizable Interior-Point ADMM for Block-Structured Nonconvex Programs
summary: Physics simulation is an increasingly important computational primitive for AI, and local--global/ADMM splitting exposes its parallel structure but lacks matching finite-time convergence guarantees. We close this gap with two ADMM variants, Interior-Point ADMM (IP-ADMM), for block-structured nonconvex composite programs with smooth nonlinear inequality and affine constraints. A one-sided finite-activation wall keeps each constraint split state strictly feasible while the original-space infeasibility vanishes, giving closed-form constraint updates, one proximal call per objective block, and one equality-constrained quadratic consensus solve per iteration. \rev{To our knowledge, this makes IP-ADMM the first single-loop method that updates nonconvex inequality constraints locally and in parallel with finite-time convergence guarantees.} Ordinary IP-ADMM attains a CQ-free best-iterate weak-KKT rate of $O(K^{-1/3})$ or a banded Fritz--John rate of $O(K^{-1/4})$, which converts to KKT at $O(K^{-1/4})$ under a uniform constraint qualification; these are nearby-point certificates that reduce to conventional KKT for smooth blocks. A checkpoint variant, IP-ADMM-Ckpt, improves the asymptotic KKT exponent to $O(K^{-1/3})$. We also show how the bounds scale with the objective- and constraint-block counts and the coupling norm.

title: Lift, See, Act: Hierarchical Robot Policy Pretraining with 3D Foundation Models
summary: Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.

title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure
summary: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/hnghiem-nlp/hirewatch_repo.

title: Model Immunization Beyond Condition Numbers: The Importance of Plateau Regions
summary: Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly compromise safety alignment in Large Language Models, underscoring the vulnerability of deployed models to post-release modification. While prior work motivates model immunization by inducing ill-conditioned curvature to slow harmful optimization, this approach is not scalable due to the high computational cost of Hessian estimation. We refine this paradigm by extending the theoretical framework to prioritize plateau regions alongside curvature. We further introduce an immunization algorithm based on efficient Hessian estimation and bounds on the extremal singular values of the Hessian. We demonstrate the proposed immunization framework in three applications: (i) Fine-tuning-as-a-service settings where benign user data may be mixed with poisoned harmful data, (ii) open-weight settings where an adversary can fine-tune on harmful-only data with varied training dynamics, and (iii) robust unlearning, where immunized models better resist relearning attacks after unlearning. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach achieves robust defense against adversarial fine-tuning while largely maintaining general utility and downstream trainability. Our code is available at https://github.com/minhquoc0712/BECON.

title: Beyond Semantic Prompts: Unified Watermarking and Access Control for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion services require both traceability of generated content and differentiated access to generation capabilities. However, existing watermarking methods commonly expose watermark control through mechanisms beyond the text-prompt interface, while credential-based access control does not inherently enforce distinct output quality levels. We propose a unified framework that enables customizable multi-bit watermark embedding and tiered access control through a single text prompt. A unified prompt represents watermark messages using designated words and associates protocol structures with different access states. The framework adopts a two-stage training strategy. First, watermark payload partitioning represents messages as designated watermark words, while vocabulary extension assigns each protocol word a dedicated token with a learnable input embedding. Guided by a frozen reference model and a pretrained watermark codec, joint adaptation of the U-Net and protocol-token embeddings transfers message-dependent watermark patterns into the generation process. Second, a prompt-structure recognition network controls feature modulation within the variational autoencoder decoder, which is trained to produce clear watermarked images, blurred previews, or black outputs according to the access state. Experiments demonstrate reliable watermark recovery, robustness to common image-processing operations and evaluated model modifications, and consistent performance across diverse generation settings. The controlled decoder also achieves distinct output behaviors under restricted access while closely preserving reference decoding fidelity and watermark recoverability under full access. Our open-source code and model weights will be public after acceptance.

title: ReRead: Wrong Predictions, Useful Representations - Correcting Frozen Robot Policies by Re-reading Their Own Representations
summary: When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module. We argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations: a policy can retain the required information yet fail to read it out as the correct action. To test this view, we propose ReRead: with the backbone frozen, a corrector re-reads the current and two previous caches to predict an action residual. The corrector sees no images, is trained solely on offline demonstrations from all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and adds only 4.17% latency. Ablations and interventions show that the correction relies on the backbone's own representations: none of four external visual encoders adds further gain, and swapping in past caches from other trajectories sharply increases action error. On the 11 hardest RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, ReRead improves the success rates of LingBot-VLA, $π_{0.5}$, and Fast-WAM by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, it raises Fast-WAM's average success rate from 90.73% to 92.66%. On a Flexiv dual-arm robot, it raises success on a phase-ambiguous task from 0% to 36%.

title: LiveView: Real-Time Camera-Controlled Re-filming of Streaming Videos
summary: Real-time camera-controlled video re-filming aims to synthesize target views from a streaming source video under online user-specified camera trajectories. This task poses two key challenges: maintaining synchronization and content consistency across views, and achieving low-latency rendering with long-horizon stability. Existing approaches are predominantly designed for offline full-sequence processing and rely on bidirectional attention or costly depth-based geometric preprocessing, making them unsuitable for low-latency streaming scenarios. To address these limitations, we develop a teacher-to-student framework that distills a high-fidelity bidirectional re-filming teacher into a few-step causal autoregressive student. We introduce Cross-Frame Injection to interleave each incoming source frame with its synchronized target latent, thereby establishing direct cross-view correspondence and improving content consistency. To ensure stable long-horizon generation, we further propose Shared Relative RoPE, which bounds temporal indices within the pretrained range, and Cycle Streaming Tuning, which exposes the student to extended cyclic trajectories during streaming training. These designs enable low-latency online video re-filming with precise camera control and sustained spatiotemporal consistency over long streaming rollouts.

title: Stochastic Self-Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in robotics through imitation learning, yet fine-tuning them with on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited. In group-based RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), every rollout step requires multi-step ODE integration, and the sampler's limited stochasticity leads to rollout groups with low variance. We propose VLA-SSD, which addresses both high inference latency and limited stochasticity. In particular, our method self-distills a pretrained flow-matching action head into a stochastic one-step policy by conditioning a single-jump generator on a Brownian path. We derive a conditional action density via our stochastic one-step policy, enabling efficient post-training via likelihood-ratio RL algorithms. We show that distilling VLA-SSD from the $π_0$ VLA reduces the action head's forward-pass time by a factor of 7.7, at the cost of a 5.5% relative decrease in the success rate on the LIBERO benchmark. However, by leveraging the increased sample diversity of VLA-SSD during group generation, post-training a $π_{0.5}$ VLA using GRPO yields a 20.6% relative improvement.

title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
summary: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with \texttt{grep}. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over $91$ repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

title: Generative AI-Driven Parametric Design Optimization Framework for Vehicle Closure Systems
summary: This study presents a generative AI-driven parametric design optimization framework integrating performance-oriented generation with editable computer-aided design (CAD) and downstream computer-aided engineering (CAE) analysis for industrial vehicle closure systems. The framework is demonstrated on an automotive tailgate assembly with complex geometry, coupled components, and competing performance and feasibility requirements. A production-oriented CATIA model is restructured into a reference-based parametric template with a 13-dimensional design representation. An automated CAD/CAE workflow generates parametric models, performs structural analysis, and constructs a database of mass, maximum displacement, and maximum von Mises stress. Gaussian process regression surrogates predict performance, while diffusion and flow matching models generate design candidates. The design problem minimizes mass and maximum displacement, with stress assessed as an engineering feasibility constraint. Performance-guided generation using surrogate guidance and performance-aware training using a performance-aware loss incorporate engineering objectives, with sensitivity to guidance scale and loss weight evaluated. Generative search is compared with NSGA-II under matched evaluation budgets using a common surrogate model. Selected Pareto-region candidates are reconstructed in CATIA and re-evaluated through native CAE; all verified candidates are successfully regenerated and analyzed. Relative to the baseline, the knee-point design reduces mass by 7.1% and maximum displacement by 29.4%, while extreme verified solutions achieve maximum reductions of 10.3% and 37.3%, respectively. The results demonstrate performance-oriented multi-objective design exploration compatible with editable industrial CAD and native engineering verification.

title: MAGE: Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence for Transferable Multimodal Graph Learning
summary: Multimodal graphs integrate textual and visual attributes with relational structures, providing a rich representation of complex real-world data. To enable the broad applicability and reuse of graph models, it is crucial for models trained on source graphs to generalize to unseen graph domains. However, this is challenging because cross-modal interactions among neighbors and the neighboring information needed for prediction can vary across target nodes and graph domains. This gives rise to two key challenges: adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion, which captures and integrates cross-modal interactions among neighbors to accommodate variations across nodes and domains; and target-specific evidence selection, which identifies the neighboring textual and visual information needed for each target node to support LLM-based prediction. In light of these challenges, we propose MAGE (Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence Prompting), a framework for transferable multimodal graph learning. MAGE represents textual and visual node views separately in a heterogeneous graph and introduces two complementary components. Meta-path Adaptive Multimodal Propagation (MAMP) adaptively aggregates neighborhood information along heterogeneous meta-paths and compresses it into graph-aware soft tokens. Evidence-Guided Instruction Tuning (EGIT) selects relevant neighboring evidence for each query and incorporates its graph-aware representations into instructions for a frozen multimodal LLM. Together, these components support transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without target-domain parameter updates. Experiments with three source graphs and four unseen target graphs demonstrate strong cross-domain transfer performance on node classification and link prediction, without requiring parameter updates on the target domains.

title: Multimodal Violence Understanding and Temporal Retrieval in Movies with Adaptive Audio-Visual Fusion
summary: Violence in films and streaming media remains a concern for audience protection and creates substantial workload for manual content classification. Existing violence-detection methods often rely on limited modalities or short video clips, making it difficult to capture complementary evidence and localise violent events in long, untrimmed videos. In this study, we develop a framework for multimodal video understanding that classifies violence severity, predicts multiple violence types, and locates violent events in time. We combine temporally aligned visual and audio features extracted using pretrained encoders through attention-based adaptive fusion, followed by Transformer-based temporal modelling. Our framework supports three complementary tasks: video-level violence-severity classification, multi-label violence-type prediction, and temporal localisation of violent events. We evaluate the framework on the XD-Violence benchmark and examine its cross-domain performance using AIRTLab. On XD-Violence, our multimodal model achieves 93.27\% severity-classification accuracy and a micro-F1 score of 88.60\% for multi-label violence-type prediction, outperforming the corresponding unimodal configurations. We achieve a mean temporal intersection-over-union (tIoU) of 0.5075 for temporal localisation. Our cross-domain experiments reveal performance degradation under different recording conditions, while our movie case studies demonstrate the framework's potential to retrieve potentially violent scenes for further review. Our results highlight the practical value of multimodal intelligent systems in supporting human reviewers with the identification, classification, and temporal retrieval of violent content in films and streaming media.

title: The Logic Chain Breaking Point: A Controlled-Variable Benchmark for Reasoning Degradation in Open-Weight Language Models
summary: We introduce The Logic Chain Breaking Point, a controlled-variable benchmark for deductive reasoning in open-weight language models. It spans three phases: (i) pure modus-ponens chain scaling, (ii) distractor resilience with a fixed core chain, and (iii) contradiction detection under primacy versus recency placement. Independent variables follow a powers-of-two sequence $v \in \{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}$, with ground truth known by construction. We evaluate sixteen open-weight models across instruction-tuned and reasoning-tuned panels, including a small-model suite and a larger local-model extension. All models are evaluated with greedy decoding under model-appropriate context and output budgets, while context- and length-limited trials are quarantined from the valid accuracy denominator. Our results reveal a sharply non-monotonic difficulty surface: pure deductive chains up to $L=128$ remain near saturation for most models, and distractor noise causes only model-specific degradation at high $D$, while the inconsistent premise condition has the lowest accuracy. Instruction-tuned models, including larger 24B--27B baselines, score essentially zero on inconsistent premise sets, while reasoning-tuned models recover only partially and remain below reliable accuracy. Within this benchmark, inconsistent premise sets are associated with the strongest degradation under the benchmark's abstention-based scoring rule.

title: Overview of the Plagiarism Detection Task at PAN 2026
summary: The generative plagiarism detection task at PAN 2026 aims at retrieving the original scientific sources for given automatically generated textual plagiarism. We created two novel datasets of synthetically generated plagiarism following the premise of a malicious actor trying to generate papers with minimal effort while evading detection of undisclosed re-use. We utilized four widely available LLMs: GPT-OSS 120B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 3.5 27B FP8, and DeepSeek-R1 Distill Llama 8B. In this task overview paper, we outline the creation of this dataset and summarize and compare the results of all participants with three baselines. For this year's task, we received 26 submissions from six teams that significantly outperformed our baselines.

title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
summary: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

title: Joint Antenna Positioning and Dynamic Beam Tracking for MA-Enabled Full-Duplex Secure ISAC Systems: A Flow Matching DRL Approach
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) improves spectral efficiency but faces significant security challenges in dynamic wireless environments, where the potential eavesdropper is treated as the sensing target. This paper proposes a movable antenna (MA)-enabled full-duplex secure ISAC system that tracks the mobile eavesdropper while safeguarding both uplink and downlink transmissions. Specifically, an extended Kalman filter (EKF) is employed to recursively estimate and predict the eavesdropper's state from radar echoes. Building on the estimated target state, we formulate a joint optimization problem to maximize the sum of the uplink and downlink secrecy rates by jointly optimizing the transmit and receive MA positions, uplink and downlink beamforming, artificial noise, and uplink transmit power. The resulting problem is challenging due to its inherent nonconvexity, strong coupling among optimization variables, and time-varying nature. Conventional iterative optimization methods may incur prohibitive computational overhead in dynamic environments, whereas existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods based on unimodal Gaussian or deterministic policies may struggle to capture complex multimodal high-reward action distributions. To address these challenges, we develop a flow matching-based deep reinforcement learning (FMDRL) algorithm for sequential joint decision-making. The proposed algorithm integrates a conditional velocity-field actor with twin critics, generating continuous actions through finite-step Euler integration and employing a deterministic decoder to enforce physical constraints on antenna positions, transmit power, and positive semidefiniteness. Extensive numerical simulations confirm that the proposed FMDRL algorithm achieves superior performance in terms of both communication security and target tracking capabilities.

title: On the Convergence of Continuous-Time AdamW
summary: Continuous-time AdamW provides a framework for understanding whether an optimizer widely used to train large-scale neural networks settles to an equilibrium or sustains persistent motion. We study this long-time behavior while retaining bias correction and fixed positive weight decay. Under suitable assumptions, we establish that the dynamics are well defined for all time and remain bounded when the decay is sufficiently small. Our main result connects their limiting behavior to the geometry of the objective: trajectories approach a locally invariant manifold whose dimension equals the Hessian nullity along the associated critical component. When critical points are isolated and have at most one such direction, the trajectory converges to a single equilibrium.
