With two degenerate directions, however, bounded persistent motion can occur even for a smooth, strictly convex objective with a unique minimum. We also quantify how close the long-time trajectory remains to the critical set as weight decay decreases, without assuming convergence to a point. These results identify objective geometry as a key to understanding when continuous-time AdamW converges and when persistent motion is possible.

title: Learning from Distribution: Rethinking One-Hot Supervision for ASR and QA in Speech Language Models
summary: Speech language models (SLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and general-purpose speech understanding, yet ASR-specific training often degrades spoken question answering (QA) performance. We revisit this conflict from the perspective of task-specific input--output mappings and one-hot supervision. Our findings reveal pronounced task-asymmetric effects: ASR-only training severely limits QA capability, whereas QA-only training retains reasonable ASR performance. We hypothesize that the relatively deterministic mapping of ASR, combined with single-reference supervision, biases models toward transcription-specific behavior. Motivated by this perspective, we advocate broadening ASR learning objectives while preserving recognition accuracy. We propose Learning from Distribution (LFD), which aligns speech-conditioned predictions with the conditional output distributions of a pretrained text LLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LFD improves both ASR and QA performance, exhibits superior data efficiency, and remains effective under full-parameter fine-tuning. CoT-ASR further supports the broader applicability of our proposed supervision principle.

title: iEEG Can Help EEG: Improving Clinical Scalp EEG Analysis through Intracranial Priors
summary: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of clinical brain monitoring, making the quality of its signal fundamental to downstream tasks and models. However, that signal is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and blurred by volume conduction. Existing methods operate almost exclusively within the scalp modality, so they inherit the contamination they would need to overcome. In practice, intracranial EEG (iEEG) observes the neural activity with far higher fidelity, yet it is invasive and therefore scarce, and the two modalities are rarely recorded as pairs at scale, share no common channel space, and offer no clean ground truth to directly supervise a mapping. Motivated by the neuronal synchronization mechanism shared by the two modalities, we propose a reprogramming approach that fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freezes it as a cross-modal prior. We introduce ReBrain, a framework to transfer an iEEG-learned prior to scalp EEG, which re-expresses any scalp signal through that prior and can be inserted upstream of any downstream model with no pairing or fine-tuning. ReBrain consistently improves host models across recordings from multiple hospitals and across architecture families, and our analysis traces this gain to genuine neural structure carried by iEEG rather than to the architecture itself. This work provides evidence that a scarce clean modality can serve as a transferable prior for an abundant noisy one, offering a general recipe for cross-modal transfer among biosignals. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xianglong-Bao/ReBrain.

title: TrainExplorer: Autonomous LLM Post-Training via Plan-and-Decouple Exploration
summary: LLM-based agents can automate model post-training, accelerating progress toward recursive self-improvement. Despite their promise, existing approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) strategy lock-in that limits exploration beyond the initial strategy; and (2) coupled execution that obscures the effects of individual modifications. To address these challanges, we propose TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous post-training, that incorporates strategy planning and execution decoupling, to achieve broaden strategy exploration. First, strategy planning draws on scientific literature to construct a candidate search space of training strategies. Then, decoupled execution enables single-component interventions and attribution to guide strategy exploration. Extensive experiments on PostTrainBench demonstrate that TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex, which scores 36.23. Code will be available.

title: Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Navigation
summary: Continual robot navigation requires reinforcement learning policies to continuously adapt to new environments while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Meanwhile, explainable reinforcement learning aims to learn meaningful behavioral representations through policy interaction. However, these objectives are inherently conflicting, as continual learning emphasizes policy stability whereas explainable behavior learning requires adaptive exploration. Existing methods rarely address both simultaneously. To resolve this issue, this paper proposes a Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FECHRL) method. A two-stage behavior cloning strategy is introduced to balance rapid policy adaptation and explainable behavior evolution by progressively transitioning from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning. Furthermore, a fuzzy critic based on a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy inference system is proposed to alleviate value extrapolation errors during the transition between imitation-guided learning and autonomous exploration, thereby improving continual training stability. Experimental results on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks demonstrate that the proposed method effectively unifies continual learning capability and policy explainability within a single reinforcement learning framework, achieving stable knowledge retention and meaningful behavioral explanation.

title: FinVerify: A Verification Framework for Financial Agents
summary: Financial agents produce numerical claims that can be wrong even when their calculations execute correctly, due to mismatched reporting periods, unsupported sources, incompatible units, or incorrect financial definitions. We introduce FinVerify, an evidence-grounded framework for verifying financial agents' numerical claims. Based on an analysis of 190 incorrect trajectories from the Agent Finance Reasoning dataset, we define five error categories--temporal integrity, source fidelity, comparability, accounting integrity, and financial-model fidelity--and operationalize them as verification protocols. An LLM structures claims and supporting evidence, while deterministic validators check financial requirements; when authoritative formulas are available, Z3 checks consistency with grounded inputs. FinVerify accepts only if all applicable checks pass, rejects proven violations, and abstains when evidence is insufficient. We evaluate the framework against a Direct baseline and an LLM judge across five fixed-candidate benchmarks. On Agent Finance Reasoning, accepted-claim precision increases from 56.4% for the LLM judge to 76.7% at 81.2% coverage. On XBRLFiling, FinVerify achieves 99.8% accepted-claim precision and 97.0% decision accuracy; on FinanceBench-67, it reaches 87.9% accepted-claim precision versus 69.7% for the judge. Improvements are smaller on FinQA and TAT-QA, where authoritative evidence is limited. These results suggest that explicit, evidence-backed verification can improve financial-agent reliability while exposing trade-offs between correctness, false rejection, and abstention.

title: Reasoning Again with a Quarter of the Experts: Retry First, Then Train
summary: Removing three quarters of the routed experts from a 122B-parameter reasoning mixture-of-experts model makes it fit in a 12 GiB file, and breaks it in a specific way: on LiveCodeBench it enters verbatim reasoning loops that run to the token limit on 44 of 120 development problems, where the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization loops on none. We study how much of that loss can be recovered without changing the kept experts' quantized bytes, in three steps of increasing cost. On development problems, a sampling penalty recovers part of it. Stopping a reply when it starts to loop and drawing again recovers more on top of it, with no weight change. Our method, B, adds rank-8 trained corrections to the kept experts, loaded as an adapter, and restores two experts per layer; it is fitted layer by layer to the unpruned model's expert block on the pruned model's own activations. In a pre-registered comparison on 130 easy and medium LiveCodeBench problems that no part of the study had touched, with both arms given the same sampling penalty and the same stop-and-redraw policy, B solves 116 problems against 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]; 15 problems gained, 3 lost). A training-free weight edit aimed at the loops, tested the same way earlier, did not help. B removes more wrong answers than loops, and costs 1.7x the wall time. On two older benchmarks used as regression checks, B stays inside a pre-set 2 pp tolerance but shows no gain (HumanEval+ +0.6 pp, MBPP+ -1.9 pp). The evidence is one model, one quantization and one benchmark family; we state what it does and does not show.

title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
summary: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
summary: A new epoch for direct visualisation of accretion dynamics near a black hole's event horizon began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (EHTC) synthesised an Earth-sized aperture with millimeter radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features, with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source. Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very-long baseline interferometry (VLBI) measurements, rendering interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms, and imaging hyperparameters. Here, we apply a newly-developed independent imaging algorithm to the M87* dataset, which is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image, and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with angular diameter 42.2 +/- 1.5 microarcseconds corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 +/- 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of ~20 deg from the approaching jet.

title: When the Cheapest Feasible Router Fails: Auditing Deployment Commitments in Cost-Aware LLM Routing
summary: Cost-aware LLM routing often selects the cheapest policy meeting empirical risk and coverage constraints. Yet a router that passes an audit can violate its fixed service contract on new requests, even when candidate policies are constructed independently. We study this deployment-commitment decision with disjoint construction, audit, and test samples. Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router deploys in 91.82% of opportunities but violates the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments. We introduce Menu-Aware Routing Commitment (MARC), which qualifies policies using audit evidence and a serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, deploy a supported alternative, or defer. Its practical policywise variant (MARC-P) reduces observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost; fixed-margin and formal risk-control procedures provide competitive alternatives. Nested audits show how added evidence changes deployable policy sets, and learned semantic routing exhibits the same commitment failure. These results establish deployment commitment as a distinct operational decision connecting router evaluation, service reliability, and inference cost.

title: Augmenting Pretrained Language Models with N-gram Embeddings through Incremental Training
summary: As a new scaling technique for large language models, the n-gram embedding improves the base ability of a model while adding almost no inference cost. Mainstream research realizes it through joint training of the n-gram embedding with the backbone, which severely restricts the settings in which an n-gram embedding can be used. We therefore propose training an n-gram embedding onto an existing model through incremental training, to extend where the technique can deliver value. Specifically, we explore several settings of the n-gram embedding under incremental training---the learning rate of the embedding, the vocabulary size, and the injection position---and train an n-gram embedding onto the existing model under the best configuration. Experiments show that the best configuration under incremental training does not fully coincide with that under pretraining; moreover, the incrementally trained knowledge is written predominantly into the n-gram embedding, while the general ability of the backbone is retained throughout this training process.

title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
summary: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.

title: Implicit-Reasoning-Enabled Elastic Semantic Communications for AI-Agent Networks
summary: AI-agent networks introduce new communication demands driven by proactive interactions and autonomous task execution. Existing adaptive semantic communication schemes primarily adjust semantic representations and resource configurations within predefined processing scales and capability sets, which may be insufficient for evolving task requirements. To address this gap, we introduce elastic semantic communications (ESC), a task-driven framework that extends semantic adaptation to the runtime execution and participation of task-supporting capabilities. ESC comprises two complementary dimensions: vertical elasticity adjusts the execution intensity of existing capabilities, while horizontal elasticity reconfigures the participating capability set. The framework connects these dimensions through the expected marginal value of additional information and computation. To realize ESC, we propose an implicit-reasoning-enabled device--edge mechanism that supports variable-depth local inference through shared-parameter state updates and edge-side continuation through wireless transfer of intermediate reasoning states. Experiments on Sudoku-Extreme demonstrate that the benefits of additional inference depend on wireless conditions, while task-aware edge invocation can preserve task accuracy with substantially lower state-transfer overhead.

title: Deploying a Control-Logic LLM Assistant in Air-Gapped Power Plants: Lessons in Source Authority and Bounded Retrieval
summary: Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.

title: Collective coupling of over 100 individually trapped atoms to a single cavity mode
summary: Coupling optical tweezer arrays to high-finesse cavities provides a shared optical interface for neutral-atom registers. Scaling this interface to large tweezer arrays requires placing many traps within the coupling region of a single cavity mode while maintaining uniform trapping and site-resolved detection. Here we match a two-dimensional array of 192 optical tweezers to the coupling profile of a millimeter-scale Fabry-Perot cavity. To improve trap uniformity in the array generated by crossed acousto-optic deflectors, we combine optimization with optical feedback and atomic fluorescence feedback, achieving a mean cesium loading probability of approximately 58%. In each trial, fluorescence imaging determines whether each individual tweezer site is occupied, allowing the cavity transmission spectra to be grouped by atom number. The grouped spectra exhibit resolved normal-mode doublets, and the group with 120 imaged atoms yields an effective collective coupling of $G_{\mathrm{eff}}/(2π) = 21.30 \pm 0.23$ MHz. A model based on the calculated coupling profile and measured site loading probabilities predicts that the mean squared coupling per occupied site changes little between 97 and 120 atoms. The fitted collective coupling is therefore consistent with square-root scaling with atom number despite the spatial variation in single-atom coupling. These results provide an experimental basis for studying photon-mediated many-body dynamics and developing cavity-assisted readout and optical links between neutral-atom registers.

title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
summary: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.

title: VisDrone-ReID: A Unified Multi-Category Object Re-Identification Benchmark
summary: Object re-identification (Re-ID) benchmarks remain predominantly confined to single-category evaluations, limiting the development of unified systems capable of operating across diverse object types. This paper presents VisDrone-ReID, a unified multi-category Re-ID benchmark derived from the VisDrone2019-MOT dataset through a principled conversion pipeline. The pipeline resolves structural incompatibilities between multi-object tracking annotations and Re-ID evaluation requirements, addressing sequence-scoped identity collision, temporal redundancy, and the absence of a principled identity-level train/test split. The resulting benchmark comprises 9,516 identities and 150,016 images across ten object categories - pedestrian, people, bicycle, car, van, truck, tricycle, awning-tricycle, bus, and motor, sourced from 80 unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) sequences captured across urban environments. A leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation protocol is adopted to provide a comprehensive assessment. Baseline experiments across four representative Re-ID models spanning CNN and transformer architectures establish the first systematic performance reference on this benchmark. Results reveal a consistent Rank-1 to mAP gap across all models, suggesting that VisDrone-ReID presents a genuine retrieval challenge beyond nearest-neighbour matching. Per-category analysis identifies pedestrian as the most challenging category and reveals that vision-language pretraining provides a measurable advantage on semantically distinctive categories. VisDrone-ReID provides a consistent platform for studying multi-category object re-identification under the scale variation, viewpoint challenges, and category diversity characteristic of real-world surveillance scenarios.

title: Triple Exchange at the Cosmological Collider in Closed Form
summary: Particles with masses near the Hubble scale leave a characteristic pattern in the primordial bispectrum, turning inflation into a cosmological collider. For light fields, where this signal is largest, no closed form is known for the full shape of the quasi-single-field triple exchange. Using Feynman-integral methods, we obtain the first closed-form results, exact in the momenta, as expansions in terms of multiple polylogarithms around the massless and conformally coupled limits. We show that the template used in Planck analyses overestimates the amplitude by up to a factor of 1.8 and underestimates the mass, whereas our new template recovers both, as needed for current and upcoming CMB and galaxy surveys. We also compute the collapsed trispectrum and, combining it with the bispectrum, find that at weak mixing it bounds the self-coupling more tightly.

title: EPI-SST: Renewal-Structured State-Space Transformers for Epidemic Forecasting
summary: Epidemic forecasting supports public health decisions ranging from capacity planning to intervention timing, for which both point accuracy and calibrated uncertainty are essential. Although neural models have advanced point forecasting, producing reliable probabilistic predictions over multiple future horizons remains challenging. Renewal models encode epidemic propagation, while neural forecasters learn flexible multi-horizon representations; integrating these strengths within a probabilistic future rollout remains underexplored. We propose EPI-SST (Epidemic State Space Transformer), a probabilistic forecaster centered on an evidence-driven renewal transition. At each horizon, neural evidence produces a bounded update to an internal multiplier and advances a finite-memory renewal state that generates the future mean trajectory. A separate heteroscedastic Gaussian head controls predictive scale using a validation-selected log-variance penalty. Across four epidemic surveillance benchmarks, EPI-SST achieves the lowest pooled RMSE on every dataset, reducing RMSE by up to 14.2 percent relative to the strongest baseline. It also achieves the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at horizons h = 4, 5, 6 on every dataset, with reductions of up to 43 percent relative to the strongest probabilistic baseline. During the abnormal 2019-2020 influenza season, EPI-SST reduces CRPS by 16.9 percent and calibration error by 78.9 percent; a three-seed replication preserves its distributional lead. Ablation studies and frozen-path interventions show that the renewal transition, attention conditioning, horizon coupling, and uncertainty-scale control make complementary contributions to predictive performance.

title: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning
summary: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.

title: Formally verified harness for Shor's order finding algorithm with $O(n^{2+ε})$ gate cost
summary: It is commonly understood that factoring a general $n$-bit biprime via Shor's order finding algorithm requires $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ gates by leveraging schoolbook integer arithmetics for addition and multiplication. Recent developments in quantum arithmetic circuits leveraging recursive Toom-Cook schemes have improved the cost scaling to $O(n^{2+ε})$. Here $ε>0$ depends on algorithm implementation details of the recursive multiplication steps, which allow for a vast number of design choices. The challenge in navigating such design space also presents an opportunity for demonstrating innovative practices in quantum software engineering in the era of open agentic science. We present a formally verified harness that ingests a design specification (namely a "policy" that describes a recursive circuit design scheme) from an external source, which may be an AI agent, and produces a set of formalized proofs covering mathematical correctness of the algorithm implementation, asymptotic scaling of the end-to-end gate cost, as well as the correctness of translating the verified algorithm to a detailed circuit implementation with an intermediate representation. The harness is published as an open challenge where human researchers and AI agents can search for more efficient factoring circuits while retaining machine-checked guarantees of correctness and end-to-end asymptotic complexity.

title: Wake-Powered Spreading of Encapsulated Drops Impacting Under Liquid
summary: A drop impacting a wall in air spreads by converting its own kinetic energy into surface energy. We show that this picture fails when the wall is submerged in liquid. Millimetric perfluoropolyether drops, bare or encapsulated in an ultrathin silicone-oil shell, impacting a glass wall in water are flattened by the squeeze flow in the draining gap and shed most of their kinetic energy before impact. Nevertheless, they spread to more than twice their diameter on a water lubrication film that never ruptures, creating more surface energy than their entire kinetic and gravitational energy could supply. A two-stage energy scaling resolves this deficit. The liquid set in motion in the drop's wake supplies more than 90\% of the energy for spreading, so that the maximum spreading is governed by the Weber number of the ambient liquid rather than that of the drop. The shell acts mainly through its interfacial tension, while its biaxial-extension dissipation, negligible before impact, becomes appreciable during spreading.

title: Response-Threshold Framework for First-Peak Preservation in Noisy Grover Search
summary: Grover search is executed only after integer iterations, so noise can alter the stopping decision even when a continuous first peak remains visible. We develop a response-threshold framework separating continuous peak motion, stroboscopic geometry, and the discrete sampled-success argmax. For a Drude-Lorentz environment, linearized HEOM supplies an a priori timing coefficient and sampled-probability differentials. The first-order layer is used as a conservative screen: well-separated points retain the nominal step, whereas near-threshold points escalate to finite-$λ$ evaluation. Across 260 unique HEOM points drawn from five overlapping validation sets, it detects all 15 observed stopping changes with zero regret on the changed subset; its residual errors are 45 one-step-early calls on otherwise stable points; the 245-point stable subset has mean regret $4.42\times10^{-3}$. An empirically validated two-stage workflow escalates every observed change while avoiding 160 of 260 unique full-HEOM propagations. Same-bath NZ2 reduces early calls. A heterogeneous three-qubit circuit exhibits three stopping-transition scales, each replicated across eight marked targets, and finite-shot recovery is 96.18% overall, with failures localized to a near-degenerate boundary at $s=1.5$. A depth-refined transfer test supports the predicted local quadratic timing-to-loss relation.

title: Frac-BKT Under Mechanism Scrutiny: Response Assimilation and a Failed Fractional-Memory Test
summary: Long-horizon knowledge tracing requires more than an evocative memory mechanism: the implementation must assimilate observed responses non-anticipatorily, and the mechanism must survive matched controls. We subject Frac-BKT, a BKT-style model with an elapsed-time-scaled truncated fractional history, to both tests. The repaired model predicts response $n$ from a prior mastery state and uses response $n$ only to update the posterior state for later events. A five-seed evaluation uses 676,848 ASSISTments 2017 interactions from 1,694 learners and 19,249 learner--skill trajectories, with chronological 80/10/10 suffix splits. The response-aware model reaches AUC .5860 overall, .5638 after gaps of at least 30 minutes, and .5668 after at least 14 days. Relative to the earlier non-response implementation, the gains are .0473, .0316, and .0277 AUC, respectively. However, the fractional mechanism gate fails: the full model is not better than the matched $α=1$ control and is worse than the matched $τ=0$ control by .0090 AUC on both long-gap slices. Student-cluster wild-bootstrap intervals exclude zero, both Holm-adjusted $p$-values are .00006, and all five per-seed differences favor $τ=0$. Compact AKT-, SAKT-, and DAS3H-style references also remain stronger on long gaps. The contribution is therefore a response-assimilation repair and a falsifiable audit showing that response assimilation helps while the evaluated fractional-history term does not---not a state-of-the-art or causal-retention claim.

title: Spectral Landmarks: Alignment of Landmark Kernel Translates with the Leading Eigenfunctions of a Kernel Operator
summary: We study the problem of choosing $m$ landmark points so that the span of the kernel translates is as close as possible to the leading $s$-dimensional eigenspace of a positive-definite kernel. The natural measure is the Hilbert-Schmidt operator discrepancy between the reproducing-kernel-Hilbert-space (RKHS) projectors onto the two subspaces. We give a closed form spectral alignment function in terms of the truncated Mercer kernel and relate it to the classical integrated power function (Nyström trace error) through a two-sided sandwich bound. Minimizing the function by gradient descent on the landmark coordinates produces landmark sets that are evenly spaced. Theoretical results show that optimal configurations are those whose eigenfunction sampling matrix is a scaled isometry. On homogeneous spaces these are exactly the minimal equal-weight cubature rules for products of leading eigenfunctions, and for every $m\ge s$ they are the configurations whose sampled eigenfunctions form a unit-norm tight frame. Experiments on $\mathbb{S}^1$ and $\mathbb{S}^2$ agree with the theory. On the circle, with $s\le2m$ and a moderate bandwidth, every random start converges to equispaced landmarks, and on the sphere the optimizer recovers the regular tetrahedron, octahedron, and icosahedron from random starts. Finally, we analyze the numerical conditioning of the problem.
